questions.title: What are Micro Frontends?
questions.quick: Micro Frontends split a large web frontend into independently owned business domains, such as vehicle discovery, finance or account. Each domain can be built, tested and often deployed on its own, yet users see one seamless site. It is the frontend counterpart of microservices: the point is clear ownership and loose coupling between teams, not just smaller code. I would only adopt it when team scale and release independence justify the extra operational complexity.
questions.revision: Micro Frontends: a frontend split into independently owned, independently deployable business domains that users experience as one application. Goal is team autonomy, not smaller code.
questions.detailed:
**Micro Frontends are an architectural style where a large frontend is divided into vertical slices, each owned by a team that is responsible for a business capability end to end.** Each slice can be developed, tested and (usually) released on its own, while the user still sees a single, coherent site.

## How it looks in practice

Take a hypothetical global automotive website. Rather than one codebase for everything, the product is cut by business domain:

{{diagram:domains}}

Each domain team owns its UI, its client-side logic, its tests, its pipeline and typically its slice of the backend contract. A thin integration layer (the shell) stitches the domains into one page or one navigation flow.

## Key ideas

- **Vertical slices, not horizontal layers.** A team owns everything from UI to API contract for a domain, instead of one team owning "all the buttons".
- **Independent delivery.** A change in the finance domain should not force a rebuild or release of the vehicle domain.
- **Explicit contracts.** Domains talk through documented interfaces (URLs, events, APIs), not by reaching into each other's internals.
- **One user experience.** Shared design tokens, accessibility rules and navigation keep the site consistent.

## Common mistakes

- Treating it as a code-organisation trick for a small team; a modular monolith is cheaper.
- Splitting by technical component (header, table) rather than by business domain.
- Forgetting the cost: more pipelines, version management and distributed debugging.

Micro Frontends are a means to organisational scalability. If your problem is not "many teams blocking each other", it is probably not the right tool.

questions.title: Why adopt Micro Frontends? What problem do they actually solve?
questions.quick: The main driver is not bundle size but organisational and deployment scalability. With a hundred developers in one repository and one deployment pipeline, every team is coupled to every other: shared release trains, merge conflicts, a broken build blocking everyone. Micro Frontends give each domain team its own codebase, pipeline and release cadence, so teams move independently. If you do not have that coordination pain, the benefit disappears and only the cost remains.
questions.revision: The real problem is people and release coupling, not code size. Micro Frontends trade technical simplicity for team autonomy and independent deployment.
questions.detailed:
**The core problem Micro Frontends solve is coordination cost between many teams working on one frontend, not the raw size of the code.** A big application can be perfectly healthy with one team; a modest one can be painful with ten.

## The coupled monolith

When many developers share a single application, a single repository and a single deployment, several things happen:

- Every release needs cross-team coordination, so teams ship on the slowest team's schedule.
- A failing test or broken build in one area blocks unrelated work.
- Shared code gets edited by everyone, so changes ripple unpredictably.
- Upgrading a framework is an all-or-nothing project.

{{diagram:coupling}}

## What the split buys

- **Ownership:** a team owns a business capability and is accountable for it.
- **Release independence:** the finance team ships on Tuesday without waiting for the offers team.
- **Technology evolution:** domains can upgrade at their own pace (within governance limits).
- **Blast-radius control:** a defect is more likely to be contained to one domain.

## What it costs

Independent deployment introduces runtime integration, version compatibility, duplicated dependencies and harder debugging. Those costs are paid by everyone, whether or not they use the independence.

## Decision rule

Ask: are teams routinely blocked by each other's releases? Are domain boundaries stable and understood? Is independent release a business requirement? If the answers are mostly no, invest in a modular monolith with clear module boundaries, code owners and a good CI pipeline first.

questions.title: What are the key characteristics of a good Micro Frontend architecture?
questions.quick: I look for domain-oriented ownership, independent development and deployment, explicit contracts between parts, and loose coupling. On top of that the platform needs a shared design system for a consistent experience, and failure isolation so one broken domain does not take down the page. Independence should be pursued only where justified, and governed centrally for cross-cutting standards such as accessibility, security and performance.
questions.revision: Domain ownership, independent delivery, explicit contracts, loose coupling, shared design system, failure isolation, and light central governance for cross-cutting standards.
questions.detailed:
**A healthy Micro Frontend architecture combines autonomy for teams with a small set of platform-level rules.** The source list of ten traits collapses into four groups.

## 1. Ownership and boundaries

- **Domain-oriented ownership:** each frontend maps to a business capability (finance, dealer search), not a technical widget.
- **Independent team ownership:** one team can reason about, change and operate its domain.

## 2. Delivery

- **Independent development** (own repository or clearly separated module, own tests).
- **Independent deployment** where justified, with its own pipeline and rollback.
- **Independent evolution:** dependencies and internals can change without a coordinated release, within agreed compatibility ranges.

## 3. Integration

- **Clear contracts:** the routes, events, props, exposed modules and API shapes that other parts rely on are explicit and versioned.
- **Loose coupling:** no reaching into another domain's state or DOM.
- **Failure isolation:** a runtime error or slow remote degrades one region, not the page.

## 4. Experience and governance

- **Shared design system** and tokens so the site feels like one product.
- **Consistent UX** for navigation, accessibility, analytics and error handling.
- **Governance:** agreed standards on shared dependency versions, performance budgets and observability.

## Pitfall

"Independent" is a spectrum. Teams that share a global store, deploy in lock-step or import each other's components have a distributed monolith: all the cost, little of the autonomy. A useful test is whether one domain can ship on a quiet Tuesday without telling anyone.

questions.title: Micro Frontends versus a monolithic frontend: when should you not use them?
questions.quick: A monolithic React app is one deployable with centralised ownership: easier to build, debug and reason about, ideal for small or medium teams. Micro Frontends give explicit domain boundaries and independent deployments but add operational and debugging complexity. I would not convert automatically. If one team owns the app or boundaries are weak, I would choose a modular monolith, and introduce Micro Frontends only when scale, boundaries and release independence justify it.
questions.revision: Monolith is simpler; Micro Frontends buy autonomy at the price of distributed complexity. Default to a modular monolith unless team scale and release independence demand more.
questions.detailed:
**Do not adopt Micro Frontends just because an application is large.** Choose them when organisational scale, stable domain boundaries and a need for independent releases outweigh the added complexity.

## Comparison

| Aspect | Monolithic frontend | Micro Frontends |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | One large application | Several domain frontends plus a shell |
| Deployment | Usually one unit | Potentially independent per domain |
| Coupling | Can creep in silently | Explicit boundaries (if enforced) |
| Ownership | Often central | Per business domain |
| Early-stage speed | Fast | Slower: platform work first |
| Debugging | One place, one bundle | Distributed across apps and versions |
| Best for | Small to mid teams | Many teams, long-lived products |

## When not to use them

- A single team owns the product.
- Domain boundaries are unclear or shift every quarter; you would freeze the wrong seams.
- You lack platform skills: CI/CD, observability, design-system ownership.
- Performance budgets are tight and you cannot afford duplicate runtime code.

## The middle path: modular monolith

Keep one build but enforce boundaries with folders or workspace packages, lint rules on imports, code owners and public module APIs. This captures much of the clarity and can later be cut along the same lines if independent deployment becomes necessary.

## Signals to move

Teams repeatedly block each other's releases, build and test times grow beyond tolerance, and domain ownership is already clear in the organisation. Migrate incrementally rather than rewriting.

questions.title: What is the difference between Micro Frontends and Microservices?
questions.quick: Microservices decompose backend capabilities, each service owning its logic and data behind an API. Micro Frontends decompose the user interface into independently owned domains composed by a shell. They share the idea of bounded ownership and loose coupling and complement each other well, with each domain team owning a vertical slice from UI to service, but neither requires the other. You can have either one without the other.
questions.revision: Microservices split backend capabilities; Micro Frontends split frontend capabilities. Same ownership philosophy, complementary, but independently adoptable.
questions.detailed:
**Microservices split the backend into independently deployable services; Micro Frontends split the user interface into independently owned frontend domains.** They apply the same principle (bounded ownership, loose coupling) at different layers.

{{diagram:layers}}

## Side by side

| | Microservices | Micro Frontends |
|---|---|---|
| Layer | Server-side capability | Browser-side experience |
| Unit | Service with its own data | Domain UI with its own build |
| Integration | HTTP/gRPC/events via gateway | Shell composition, routes, events |
| Failure handling | Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers | Error boundaries, fallbacks |
| Main pain | Distributed data and tracing | Shared runtime, bundle size, UX consistency |

## How they combine

The cleanest alignment is a **vertical slice per team**: the finance team owns the finance frontend and the finance service(s). The finance frontend talks to its own APIs, perhaps via a gateway or a backend-for-frontend, rather than calling another domain's frontend.

## They are independent choices

- Microservices with a single frontend monolith is very common; the UI becomes the new bottleneck.
- A Micro Frontend architecture over a monolithic backend is possible, though teams will eventually collide on the backend.

## Mistake to avoid

Assuming one implies the other, or mirroring services one-to-one with frontends. Frontend boundaries follow user journeys and business capabilities, which may combine several services.

questions.title: What is the biggest mistake teams make with Micro Frontends?
questions.quick: Slicing by technical component instead of business domain. A Header MFE, Button MFE, Search MFE and Table MFE gives no real ownership: every user journey needs several teams and every feature change crosses boundaries. I would slice by business capability such as vehicle discovery, finance, dealer or customer account, so a team can deliver a user-visible outcome alone. Reusable UI primitives belong in a design system library, not in separately deployed frontends.
questions.revision: Split by business domain, not by UI component. Components belong in a design system; domains belong to teams that can ship a whole feature.
questions.detailed:
**The classic failure is cutting by technical layers or widgets rather than by business domain.** The result is many tiny deployables that must all change together for any real feature.

## Bad versus better

| Technical slicing (avoid) | Domain slicing (prefer) |
|---|---|
| Header MFE | Vehicle Discovery MFE |
| Button MFE | Finance MFE |
| Search MFE | Dealer MFE |
| Table MFE | Customer Account MFE |

With widget slicing, adding "finance estimate on the vehicle page" touches four teams. With domain slicing, one team owns the full journey.

## Why it goes wrong

- Ownership is about outcomes; a button has no business owner.
- Runtime integration for tiny pieces multiplies network requests and failure points.
- Teams coordinate constantly, recreating the coupling you set out to remove.

## How to find good boundaries

- Start from **user journeys and business capabilities**, using domain-driven design bounded contexts or event storming.
- Check the org chart: boundaries that match stable teams survive.
- Look at change patterns: things that change together belong together.
- Verify data ownership: each domain should own its primary data via an API.

## Where shared UI goes

Reusable pieces such as buttons and form fields are shared through a **versioned design-system package**, consumed at build time or as a shared remote. Cross-cutting UI like global navigation belongs to the shell.

## Smell test

If shipping one customer-visible feature routinely needs coordinated releases from three or more frontends, the seams are in the wrong place.

questions.title: What is the application shell and what should it own?
questions.quick: The shell is the host application that loads and composes the domain frontends. It owns platform concerns: global navigation, top-level routing, authentication session, design system, error handling, analytics, feature flags, configuration, loading and fallback behaviour, and observability. I would keep business logic out of it. A shell that knows vehicle or finance rules becomes a new monolith and a bottleneck for every team.
questions.revision: The shell owns cross-cutting platform concerns (nav, auth, routing, errors, analytics, config) and stays thin; domain business logic lives in the domain frontends.
questions.detailed:
**The shell (or container) is the host application that boots first, provides the page chrome and platform services, and loads domain frontends into it.** Its job is composition, not business functionality.

{{diagram:shell}}

## Typical responsibilities

- **Global layout:** header, footer, primary navigation.
- **Top-level routing:** mapping URL prefixes to domains.
- **Authentication session:** sign-in handshake and exposing identity context.
- **Design system and theming:** tokens, base styles, shared components.
- **Error handling and fallbacks:** error boundaries, loading skeletons, timeouts for remotes.
- **Analytics, feature flags, configuration:** one consistent implementation.
- **Observability:** correlation IDs, error and performance reporting.
- **Loading strategy:** deciding what to prefetch or lazy-load.

## What to keep out

Vehicle pricing rules, finance eligibility checks, offer logic. If the shell must change whenever a domain adds a feature, it is a bottleneck, and the shell team becomes a gatekeeper.

## Design guidelines

- Keep the shell small, stable and highly tested; its failure takes down everything.
- Define a narrow, versioned platform API for domains (identity, config, telemetry, navigation helpers).
- Make shell deployment cheap and safe, with canary releases and fast rollback.
- Prefer configuration (a registry of domains and their entry points) over code changes to add a domain.

## Trade-off

A thicker shell gives consistency; a thinner shell gives autonomy. Place the line by asking whether a concern is truly cross-cutting.

questions.title: What are the main ways to compose Micro Frontends?
questions.quick: There are several integration points. Build-time composition publishes each domain as a package that the shell bundles, simple but couples releases. Runtime composition, for example Module Federation or loading ES modules, keeps deployments independent. Server-side or edge composition assembles HTML before it reaches the browser, good for SEO and first paint. iframes give hard isolation, and Web Components give a framework-neutral element contract. I choose by isolation, performance and team autonomy needs.
questions.revision: Composition options: build-time packages, runtime module loading, server or edge assembly, iframes, Web Components. Trade integration depth and performance against deployment independence and isolation.
questions.detailed:
**Micro Frontends are an architecture; there are several technical ways to compose the pieces.** Pick based on how independent the releases must be and how deeply the pieces must integrate.

| Strategy | How it works | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|---|
| Build-time (npm packages) | Shell imports domain packages and builds one bundle | Simple, shared deps are natural, great performance | Shell must rebuild and redeploy for every domain change; weak independence |
| Runtime via module loading (e.g. Module Federation, native ES modules with import maps) | Shell loads remote bundles in the browser | Independent deploys, deep integration, shared libraries | Version-compat risk, runtime failure modes, more tooling |
| Server-side / edge composition | Server or CDN stitches HTML fragments (for example with SSI or ESI-style includes) | Fast first render, SEO friendly, works without client JS | Infrastructure complexity, interactivity needs hydration |
| iframes | Each domain in its own browsing context | Strongest isolation, any technology, safe for third parties | Awkward routing, sizing, accessibility and communication; weaker UX integration |
| Web Components | Each domain exposed as a custom element | Framework-agnostic contract, style encapsulation via Shadow DOM | Still need a loading mechanism; SSR and form/a11y quirks |

## Choosing

- Public, SEO-sensitive content with moderate interactivity: consider server or edge composition for the page frame, with client-side islands.
- Authenticated app-like experiences built in one framework: runtime module loading.
- Untrusted or legacy code that must be sandboxed: iframes.
- Mixed frameworks: Web Components as the contract.

These can be combined: server-rendered shell, Web Component contracts, and federated modules for interactive parts.

## Common mistake

Choosing the technology first. Decide the independence, isolation and SEO requirements, then select the mechanism.

questions.title: What is the difference between Micro Frontends and Web Components?
questions.quick: Micro Frontends are an architectural approach about how teams and domains are split. Web Components are a browser standard for custom elements, Shadow DOM and templates. They are different categories: Web Components can be one technology for implementing Micro Frontends, alongside Module Federation, iframes, server-side composition or build-time composition. In short, Web Components are a technology; Micro Frontends are an architecture.
questions.revision: Web Components are a browser technology; Micro Frontends are an architecture. Web Components can implement the contract, but do not provide ownership or deployment independence by themselves.

questions.title: iframes versus Module Federation: how do you choose?
questions.quick: An iframe gives strong isolation: separate document, CSS, JavaScript and failure domain, ideal for third-party or legacy content, but routing, sizing, accessibility and communication are harder. Module Federation loads modules into the host at runtime, giving deep integration, shared dependencies and a smoother UX, but less isolation. I prefer Module Federation for tightly integrated first-party experiences and iframes when isolation or third-party ownership outweighs integration.
questions.revision: iframe equals hard isolation and awkward integration; Module Federation equals deep integration and shared runtime but weaker isolation. Choose by trust and coupling needs.
questions.detailed:
**Use Module Federation (or similar native composition) for tightly integrated first-party experiences, and iframes when strong isolation or third-party ownership matters more than seamless UX.**

{{diagram:compare}}

## Comparison

| Concern | iframe | Module Federation |
|---|---|---|
| JS and CSS isolation | Strong, separate browsing context | Shared page; must manage conflicts |
| Crash blast radius | Contained | Contained only with error boundaries |
| Shared dependencies | None; each iframe loads its own | Can share React and others |
| Routing and deep links | Manual syncing with parent URL | Natural in host router |
| Layout | Fixed size or resize messaging | Participates in normal layout |
| Communication | postMessage, explicit and serialisable | Props, events, shared modules |
| Accessibility | Focus and landmark challenges | Same document, easier |
| Security | Sandbox attribute, origin separation | Same origin privileges as host |
| Performance | Duplicated runtime, extra document | Shared libs reduce duplication |

## When iframes win

- Embedding third-party or untrusted content, such as a payment widget or partner tool.
- Wrapping a legacy app you cannot modernise yet.
- Needing independent technology stacks with zero shared runtime.

## When Module Federation wins

- A cohesive product where pages and components interleave.
- Shared design system and React runtime.
- Performance-sensitive flows where duplicate frameworks hurt.

## Mistake

Using iframes to avoid design work on contracts, then fighting resize, focus management and analytics for years. Equally, treating federation as isolation: a federated remote runs with the host's privileges.
